cover.description: A themed title page; optional subtitle, logo and metadata collapse when omitted.

running-head.description: Document title in the header and confidentiality, page fields and date in the footer, inherited by every later section; those sections continue on the page.

key-takeaways.description: Executive conclusions with bounded one-line takeaways. Copy and adapt this document-local example.

source-line.description: A hairline and a source line in the source role, under a figure or a table. The data blocks invoke it; copy it to add a source to anything else.

kpi-row.description: Two to four headline metrics in equal columns: value with its unit, label, and a signed delta with a direction glyph; four of them set the figures a size smaller. An optional source collapses with its hairline. Text budgets reject overflow; columns reflow at unchanged type size.

unit.description: Suffix drawn after the figure at half its size: %, €m, pts. Write the space yourself when one belongs.

delta.description: Signed change shown beside the figure: +3.2 pts, −0.4.

trend.description: Direction glyph drawn before the delta.

figure-caption.description: The numbered caption under a figure: **Figure N.** and the text, N being a Word SEQ field over the figure sequence. chart-figure and figure invoke it, so charts and images number together.

chart-figure.description: A numbered, sourced chart: the chart itself (highcharts through the export server, or a native chart on the office-open renderer), a caption that says what it shows, an optional takeaway beneath, and the source line the report cites. The source is required; the figure number is a Word SEQ field.

chart.description: A highcharts or chart component. Put the unit in the value-axis title: Revenue (€m).

caption.description: What the chart shows, as a statement: Revenue by quarter, 2026.

takeaway.description: The one sentence the reader should leave with.

data-table.description: A sourced numeric table: a title, a text column of row labels at a fifth of the measure, one to five data columns right-aligned by construction, then optional notes and a source line. With its header, 24 rows keep the table on one page; the table-design rule checks the compiled table for mixed decimals.

labels.description: Row labels, top to bottom. Every data column lists its cells in this order and at this count.

header.description: Column header; put the unit here: Revenue (€m).

cells.description: One formatted value per row label, rounded the same way down the column.

numeric.description: Right-align header and cells so digits line up by place value. Set false for a text column.

notes.description: What the reader needs to interpret the figures: definitions, periods, exclusions.

callout.description: An aside set off by a hairline rule down its left edge: a short label over up to sixty words of text. No fill, so it reads as a note beside the argument rather than a box in it.

footnotes.description: Notes and sources: every distinct source-role slot value the document's block invocations carry, in order, as a numbered list under a label — the engine's /sources context. Emits nothing when no invocation cites a source.

metadata.title: Workforce Plan: Scaling to 400 by FY2029
metadata.author: Paolo Barbato

slots.title: Workforce Plan: Scaling to 400 by FY2029
slots.subtitle: Closing the hiring gap through retention and pyramid mix

items: Hiring at today's rate fills only 62% of the 307 hires needed through FY2029 — the rest must come from retention or mix.
Staff in years three to five leave at 26%, nearly double the firm average, and drive most attrition-related hiring need.
Cut 3–5 year attrition to 18%, shift the pyramid younger, and reach 400 staff by FY2029 for about $5.5m.

slots.source: Recruiting run-rate and HR attrition system, trailing 12 months to Aug 2026.

props.text: Growing from 240 to 400 staff by FY2029 means adding 160 net people while attrition keeps taking people out the other side. Blended attrition runs at 17% a year, but it is not evenly spread: staff in their third to fifth year leave at 26%, nearly double the firm-wide rate, and that single band of tenure accounts for the majority of all leavers even though it holds little more than a third of headcount. Hiring at the current rate — the pace the recruiting engine has delivered over the past two years — fills only 62% of the gross hires the plan requires each year. The remaining 38% has to come from somewhere else: either fewer people leave, or the mix of junior to senior hires changes so the engine can source faster than it does today.

The bridge below carries the firm from 240 to 400 over three years. Each year states the starting headcount, the people attrition removes, the gross hires required to hit the year's target, how many of those the current hiring rate delivers on its own, and how many more the retention and mix-shift levers below have to supply to close the rest. The shortfall is front-loaded in absolute hires but back-loaded in difficulty: year three needs the most additional hires precisely when the easiest wins from mix-shift are already spent, which is why the retention program has to be running at full strength by then, not started then.

slots.caption: Headcount grows from 240 today to 400 by FY2029, net of attrition each year
slots.takeaway: Year three requires the most new hires of any year, right when attrition and growth both peak together.

props.text: The table below sets out the same three years as a bridge: starting headcount, attrition, the hires the current recruiting rate delivers on its own, and the additional hires retention and mix-shift have to supply to close the rest.

slots.title: Headcount bridge: starting headcount, attrition, hires and ending headcount by year
slots.notes: Base hires are what today's recruiting engine delivers on its own (62% of gross hires required); plan hires are the additional hires the retention and mix-shift levers supply beyond that base.

props.text: The 3-5 year band is where the plan buys back the most hires for the least cost, because every point of attrition avoided there is a hire the firm never has to source, screen or onboard. The retention plan targets that band directly: a structured compensation and promotion review at the three-year mark, before people start looking elsewhere; a technical track that lets senior engineers grow without moving into management; a retention pool that vests at year five for high performers in the band; and a quarterly attrition-risk review that practice leads own, not HR alone. The target is to bring 3-5 year attrition down from 26% to 18% by the end of year three, and blended attrition from 17% to 14%.

slots.title: Attrition by tenure band, current vs. FY2029 target
slots.source: HR attrition system, trailing 12 months to Aug 2026; FY29 figures are plan targets.
slots.notes: Blended rates weight each band by its share of headcount; the mid-tenure band drives the gap.

slots.label: Why this band
slots.text: Staff in years three to five are old enough to be fully billable and experienced enough to be recruited away, but not yet far enough along the promotion track to feel the firm is investing back in them — the retention plan closes that gap directly.

props.text: The other lever is the mix. The 62% fill rate is not a uniform shortfall — it concentrates in senior lateral hires, which are scarce, slow to source, and where the firm competes hardest. Junior and graduate hiring can scale faster. The plan expands graduate and campus intake, builds an internal promotion pipeline from the 3-5 year band into senior roles (funded by the retention program above), adds a small contractor bench for year-one delivery risk, and invests in employer brand and referrals to lift the fill rate from 62% toward 74% by year three. The pyramid shifts modestly: from 35% junior / 35% mid / 30% senior today toward 38% / 34% / 28% by FY2029.

The retention and mix-shift levers cost an estimated $5.5 million over three years: $3.0 million in incremental recruiting above the current replacement-only baseline, and $2.5 million in retention investment — compensation adjustments, the year-five retention pool and the promotion pipeline — concentrated in the 3-5 year band. That compares with a current run rate of roughly $0.7 million a year spent just replacing attrition on flat headcount. It is small against what the growth itself pays for: payroll rises from roughly $36 million to $60 million a year, so $5.5 million spent once is under a quarter of one year's incremental payroll.

slots.title: Incremental cost of the plan vs. the current run rate, FY2027–FY2029
slots.notes: Together, $5.5m over three years. Incremental recruiting is spend above the ~$0.7m/yr baseline of replacing attrition on a flat 240 headcount; retention investment is new spend with no prior baseline.
slots.source: Finance run-rate model and HR cost-per-hire benchmark, FY2026.
